# Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?

Ya Gao Affiliation: Aalto University Email: [ya.gao@aalto.fi](mailto:)
   Zhengtao Zou Affiliation: Aalto University    Pekka Marttinen
Affiliation: Aalto University

###### Abstract

Distilling interactive LLM agents requires choosing between
teacher-generated demonstrations and student-generated experience,
corresponding broadly to off-policy and on-policy distillation. While
both have proven effective, we argue that this distinction is inherently
hierarchical: the policy that induces an interaction history need not be
the same as the policy that generates the token prefix of the current
action. We introduce a hierarchical agent distillation framework that
formalizes these two levels of on-policiness and enables explicit
control over their pairing, mixture proportions, and training schedule.
We study this problem through self-distillation, where a frozen teacher
has access to task guidance unavailable to the student, and conduct a
three-stage controlled study across three models and four interactive
environments. We find that student-induced histories paired with
teacher-generated action prefixes generally provide the strongest
standalone training signal, whereas following the student at both levels
generally performs worst. Nevertheless, fully on-policy data becomes
beneficial when incorporated into a mixture with other configurations.
Moreover, mixtures with identical teacher/student proportions at each
level can yield substantially different performance, showing that how
the two levels are paired matters beyond the overall amount of on-policy
data. Finally, front-loading fully teacher-generated contexts and
delaying fully on-policy contexts improves over a static mixture. These
findings provide practical principles for deciding where, how much, and
when agent distillation should follow the student.

| --- |
|     |

## 1 Introduction

Knowledge distillation (KD) ([Hinton et al., 2015](#bib.bib1)) is widely
used to post-train large language model (LLM) agents ([Yao et al.,
2022b](#bib.bib2)), transferring task-solving behavior from a teacher to
a student ([Zeng et al., 2024](#bib.bib10); [Kumar et al.,
2026](#bib.bib6)). In *privileged-information (PI)
distillation* ([Penaloza et al., 2026](#bib.bib3); [Alakuijala et al.,
2026](#bib.bib4)), the teacher receives task guidance unavailable to the
student, and distillation trains the student to reproduce the resulting
behavior without that guidance at deployment.

A central design choice is which policy generates the contexts used for
distillation. Off-policy approaches train on teacher-generated
trajectories ([Kang et al., 2026](#bib.bib5); [Liu et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib8)), providing coherent demonstrations but limited
exposure to states encountered by the student. On-policy distillation
(OPD) ([Agarwal et al., 2024](#bib.bib9); [Lu and Lab, 2025](#bib.bib7))
instead obtains teacher supervision on student-generated experience,
reducing training–deployment mismatch. However, student errors can
produce histories or partial actions from which even the teacher has
difficulty providing useful continuations ([Fu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib16)). Both approaches can be effective in agent
training ([Alakuijala et al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Liu et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib8); [Xiao et al., 2026](#bib.bib11); [Xu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib12)), raising a basic question: _should agent distillation
be on-policy?_

We argue that the trajectory-level notion of on-policiness commonly used
to characterize distillation methods is incomplete for interactive
agents. An agent’s training context contains two nested levels. At the
_history level_, preceding interactions determine the context and
environment state before the current action. At the _action-prefix
level_, previously generated tokens within the current action determine
the context for next-token prediction. Either level can independently
come from the teacher or the student. For example, a teacher can
generate an action from a student-induced history, while a student can
generate an action from a teacher-induced history. The relevant question
is therefore not only whether training is on-policy, but _at which level
and to what extent should distillation follow the student?_

We introduce _hierarchical agent distillation_, which independently
specifies the history source and action-prefix source. Choosing teacher
or student at each level yields four configurations, $`TT`$, $`ST`$,
$`TS`$, and $`SS`$, under a common distillation objective. This
formulation separates three design choices: _where_ the student is
followed, _how much_ each source configuration contributes to training,
and _when_ different configurations are emphasized during learning.

We study these choices through a controlled three-stage investigation.
Stage 1 isolates the effects of history and action-prefix sources and
their interaction. Stage 2 examines how the four configurations should
be paired and mixed under a fixed training budget. Stage 3 studies how
their allocation should change over training. We use self-distillation,
initializing teacher and student from the same checkpoint while
providing task guidance only to the frozen teacher, thereby controlling
for architecture, model size, and initialization. Across three backbones
and four interactive environments, we obtain the following findings:

- •
  The value of on-policy training depends on the level. Student-induced
  histories paired with teacher-generated action prefixes ($`ST`$)
  generally provide the strongest standalone performance, while fully
  on-policy training ($`SS`$) performs worst across the tested settings.
  Student histories expose the teacher to more opportunities for
  corrective supervision, whereas student-generated prefixes can
  constrain the usefulness of teacher continuations.
- •
  Pairing matters beyond the amount of on-policy data. Mixtures with
  identical proportions of student-generated histories and action
  prefixes can perform differently depending on how the two sources are
  paired. The strongest tested mixtures emphasize hybrid configurations
  while retaining contributions from both fully teacher-generated and
  fully on-policy contexts. In particular, a modest allocation to $`SS`$
  can improve mixed training despite its weak standalone performance.
- •
  The timing of data exposure matters. Front-loading $`TT`$ accelerates
  early learning, whereas delaying $`SS`$ improves later and final
  validation performance. Combining both schedules outperforms a static
  allocation throughout training and achieves the strongest final
  validation performance among the schedules tested.

## 2 Hierarchical Agent Distillation

### 2.1 Preliminaries

An interactive LLM agent alternates between generating actions and
receiving environment feedback. Let $`h`$ denote the interaction history
before the current action, including the task instruction and preceding
actions and observations. The action is generated autoregressively, and
$`u`$ denotes a token prefix within it. The student predicts the next
token according to $`\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h,u)`$. The teacher
additionally receives privileged task guidance $`g`$ and predicts
$`\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid h,u,g)`$. Distillation trains the student to match
this informed teacher while operating without $`g`$ at deployment.

The contexts $`(h,u)`$ used for distillation may be generated by either
policy. _Teacher-trajectory context distillation_ uses teacher-generated
histories and action prefixes ([Alakuijala et al., 2026](#bib.bib4)),
whereas _fully on-policy distillation_ uses student-generated histories
and prefixes and queries the teacher for supervision on these
contexts ([Agarwal et al., 2024](#bib.bib9); [Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib14)). We study self-distillation, initializing teacher and
student from the same checkpoint and keeping the teacher frozen. The
fully on-policy case therefore corresponds to on-policy
self-distillation (OPSD) ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib13)).

### 2.2 Hierarchical agent distillation framework

We decompose on-policiness into two nested choices: which policy
generates the interaction history, and which policy generates the
current-action prefix conditioned on that history. This decomposition
allows the two sources to be controlled independently, combined in
different proportions, and scheduled over training.

#### 2.2.1 Two Levels of On-Policiness

Let $`H\in\{T,S\}`$ denote the _history source_ and $`A\in\{T,S\}`$ the
_action-prefix source_, where $`T`$ and $`S`$ denote the teacher and
current student. For a fixed data-collection round, let $`d_{H}(h,g)`$
denote the distribution of histories induced by source $`H`$, and let
$`r_{A}(u\mid h,g)`$ denote the distribution of action prefixes
generated by source $`A`$ from history $`h`$. Student generation ignores
$`g`$. The history source determines the preceding interaction
trajectory, while the prefix source generates tokens only within the
selected current action; the prefix therefore always remains conditioned
on the chosen history.

Training is on-policy at the history level when $`H=S`$ and at the
action-prefix level when $`A=S`$. The four combinations are summarized
in
Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2.2.1 Two Levels of On-Policiness ‣ 2.2 Hierarchical agent distillation framework ‣ 2 Hierarchical Agent Distillation ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?").
$`TT`$ corresponds to teacher-trajectory context distillation, while
$`SS`$ recovers fully on-policy self-distillation. $`ST`$ obtains
teacher continuations at student-induced histories, analogous to expert
supervision on learner-visited states in dataset aggregation ([Ross et
al., 2011](#bib.bib15)). $`TS`$ instead generates student prefixes from
teacher-induced histories, as in prefix replay. In all four
configurations, the PI-conditioned teacher provides the distillation
target.

![Refer to caption](2610.31918v1/figures/opd.png)

Figure 1: Illustration of the four source configurations. The first
letter denotes the interaction-history source and the second the
current-action-prefix source. In all configurations, the PI-conditioned
teacher provides distillation supervision, while gradients update only
the student.

#### 2.2.2 A Common Training Objective

For configuration $`HA`$, the student minimizes

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{L}_{HA}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(h,g)\sim d_{H}}\mathbb{E}_{u\sim r_{A}(\cdot\mid h,g)}\left[\mathcal{D}\!\left(\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid h,u,g),\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h,u)\right)\right],H\in\{T,S\},A\in\{T,S\}.
``` |  | (1) |

where $`\mathcal{D}`$ is the token-level distillation divergence.
Forward KL uses $`\mathcal{D}(p,q)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)`$, and reverse
KL uses $`\mathcal{D}(p,q)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)`$. The divergence and
the two context sources are separate choices.

Operationally, we select a history from source $`H`$, generate the
current action from source $`A`$, and evaluate teacher–student agreement
along its token prefixes. The sampled context and teacher outputs are
treated as fixed during each update; gradients are applied only to the
student’s next-token distribution. The same supervision rule therefore
applies to all four configurations.

#### 2.2.3 Mixtures and Curricula

Let $`w_{HA}\geq 0`$ denote the weight of configuration $`HA`$, with
$`\sum_{H,A}w_{HA}=1`$. A training mixture minimizes

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{w}(\theta)=\sum_{H,A\in\{T,S\}}w_{HA}\mathcal{L}_{HA}(\theta).
``` |  | (2) |

The marginal weight on student histories is $`\alpha=w_{ST}+w_{SS}`$,
and that on student action prefixes is $`\beta=w_{TS}+w_{SS}`$. Holding
$`\alpha`$ and $`\beta`$ fixed while changing the joint weights changes
only how the two source choices are paired. For example, when
$`\alpha=\beta=\frac{1}{2}`$, equal weights on $`TT`$ and $`SS`$ form a
*diagonal* mixture, equal weights on $`ST`$ and $`TS`$ form a *crossed*
mixture, and equal weights on all four configurations form an
*independent* mixture. These mixtures have identical marginal
on-policiness but different source pairings.

Finally, allowing the weights to vary with training progress,
$`w=w^{(k)}`$, defines a curriculum. Schedules with matched cumulative
configuration weights isolate *when* each type of context is most
useful. The framework therefore separates three choices: *where* to
follow the student, *how much* each source configuration contributes,
and *when* each should be emphasized.

## 3 Setup of Controlled Study

### 3.1 Models and Benchmarks

We use Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib17)), and
Ministral-3-14B-Instruct-2512 ([Liu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib18)),
abbreviated as Ministral-3. For each backbone, teacher and student are
initialized from the same checkpoint; the teacher remains frozen
throughout training. We disable thinking mode for Qwen3.

We evaluate on ToolQA ([Zhuang et al., 2023](#bib.bib19)),
OfficeBench ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib20)), ALFWorld ([Shridhar et
al., 2021](#bib.bib21)), and WebShop ([Yao et al., 2022a](#bib.bib22)).
Following [Alakuijala et al. (2026)](#bib.bib4), ToolQA and OfficeBench
use train/validation/test splits of 646/107/323 and 191/9/86 tasks. For
ALFWorld, we stratify by task type to sample 3,000 training and 200
validation tasks from the original training pool and retain the original
evaluation split. For WebShop, we sample 3,000 training and 200
validation tasks and use the full 500-task test set. Further details are
in
Appendix [A.1.2](#A1.SS1.SSS2 "A.1.2 Benchmarks ‣ A.1 Additional details on experiment setup ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?").

##### Privileged information construction.

The teacher receives task guidance describing general solution
strategies, tool-use tips, and common failure modes. For ToolQA and
OfficeBench, we initialize guidance from [Alakuijala et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib4) and refine it with Qwen3-32B using failed
guidance-conditioned rollouts. For ALFWorld, we manually draft guidance
per task type from failed student trajectories, use it to obtain
successful Qwen3-32B trajectories, and let GPT-5.4 refine the guidance
from both successes and failures. For WebShop, we manually draft
guidance from 50 failed trajectories, organize it by decision stage and
constraint pattern, and refine it with GPT-5.4 using corresponding
successful Qwen3-32B trajectories. Examples are provided in
Appendix [A.1.1](#A1.SS1.SSS1 "A.1.1 Privileged information examples ‣ A.1 Additional details on experiment setup ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?").

### 3.2 Training Setup

##### Agent architecture.

Agents follow a ReAct-style interaction format ([Yao et al.,
2022b](#bib.bib2)): at each step, the model generates a reasoning
segment followed by an operation conditioned on the interaction history.
Operations invoke tools, execute Python code, or issue
environment-specific commands.

##### Data collection and refresh.

Before training, we collect one trajectory from the initial student and
cache three trajectories from the frozen teacher for each training and
validation task. Student trajectories provide $`SS`$ examples; $`ST`$
retains their histories but regenerates the current action with the
teacher. A randomly selected cached teacher trajectory provides $`TT`$
examples and the histories for $`TS`$, whose current actions are
generated by the student. After each training round, we refresh all
student-dependent data using the latest student: we regenerate student
trajectories for $`SS`$, teacher continuations at those histories for
$`ST`$, and student continuations at cached teacher histories for
$`TS`$. $`TT`$ continues to sample from the three cached teacher
trajectories.

##### Training exercises.

Each exercise consists of an interaction history and one current action.
We uniformly sample eight action positions per source trajectory, with
replacement when necessary, so each task contributes the same number of
exercises. Distillation conditions on the history and supervises tokens
in the current action.

##### Optimization.

We apply rank-128 LoRA adapters to all linear layers. Training runs for
eight rounds, refreshing student-dependent data between rounds. Each
round contains 32, 16, 96, and 96 gradient updates for ToolQA,
OfficeBench, ALFWorld, and WebShop, respectively, with global batch size
64. Full hyperparameters are in
Appendix [A.1.3](#A1.SS1.SSS3 "A.1.3 Training data statistics and hyperparameter settings ‣ A.1 Additional details on experiment setup ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?").

### 3.3 Evaluation

We evaluate each trained student on every test task with three trials.
The maximum action counts for ToolQA, OfficeBench, ALFWorld, and WebShop
are 15, 15, 32, and 15, respectively. We report mean success rate (SR),
pass@3 (the fraction of tasks solved in at least one trial), and mean
action count over all trajectories. For WebShop, we additionally report
the official Task Score, averaged across trials, which gives partial
credit for satisfying task requirements. Decoding settings are listed in
Table [4](#A1.T4 "Table 4 ‣ A.1.3 Training data statistics and hyperparameter settings ‣ A.1 Additional details on experiment setup ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?").

### 4.1 Main Results

Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4 Stage 1: Separating the Two Levels of On-Policiness ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?")
reports results with forward KL. All four configurations substantially
improve over the initial student, but their relative performance reveals
a consistent distinction between the two levels.

##### The effect of student histories depends on the action-prefix source.

Replacing teacher histories with student histories generally improves
success rate when prefixes are teacher-generated ($`TT\rightarrow ST`$),
but consistently hurts when prefixes are student-generated
($`TS\rightarrow SS`$). Likewise, teacher prefixes provide little
advantage on teacher histories ($`TT`$ vs. $`TS`$: at most 1.9 points),
but substantially outperform student prefixes on student histories
($`ST`$ vs. $`SS`$: 3.6–14.4 points). Thus, student-induced histories
are most effective when paired with teacher-generated actions.

##### $`ST`$ performs best overall, while $`SS`$ is weakest standalone.

$`ST`$ achieves the highest success rate in 10 of 12 settings, the
highest pass@3 in all 12, and the highest WebShop Task Score for all
three backbones. The two exceptions are ToolQA, where $`TT`$ exceeds
$`ST`$ by 0.6 points for Qwen3-8B and Ministral-3, although $`ST`$ still
attains higher pass@3. In contrast, $`SS`$ has the lowest success rate
and pass@3 among distilled variants in every setting. Its average
success-rate deficit relative to $`ST`$ is larger for Qwen3-8B than
Qwen3-14B (10.2 vs. 7.7 points), indicating greater sensitivity of the
smaller model to student-generated prefixes.

##### The pattern is robust to KL direction.

Reverse-KL results in
Appendix [A.2.1](#A1.SS2.SSS1 "A.2.1 Reverse KL ‣ A.2 Experiment results ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?")
preserve the main source-level trends. Forward KL is generally similar
or better, except in some $`SS`$ settings, and is used throughout the
remaining experiments.

### 4.2 Analysis

We next examine why the source choices interact and whether
configurations that are weaker standalone nevertheless learn
complementary behaviors. Annotation protocols are described in
Appendix [A.1.4](#A1.SS1.SSS4 "A.1.4 Trajectory Annotation Protocols ‣ A.1 Additional details on experiment setup ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?").

#### 4.2.1 Supervision during data collection

##### Student histories provide richer corrective supervision ($`TT`$ vs. $`ST`$).

For each benchmark, we sample 100 training tasks and two exercises per
task. We measure *Unresolved*, the fraction of histories containing an
uncorrected earlier error; *Identified*, the fraction of unresolved
cases where the current action recognizes the error; and *Addressed*,
the fraction of identified cases receiving a resolution or appropriate
corrective step. Unresolved errors occur in 82.7–85.0% of $`ST`$
exercises but only 14.0–19.1% of $`TT`$ exercises
(Table [6](#A1.T6.fig1 "Table 6 ‣ A.2.2 Stage 1: Analysis ‣ A.2 Experiment results ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?")).
Although identification is lower under $`ST`$, identified errors are
addressed at comparable rates, giving $`ST`$ substantially more
opportunities for corrective supervision. Across training rounds,
unresolved errors decrease while the teacher identifies a larger
fraction of those remaining
(Figure [5](#A1.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ A.2.2 Stage 1: Analysis ‣ A.2 Experiment results ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?")).

##### Student prefixes constrain teacher continuations ($`ST`$ vs. $`SS`$).

We select 100 student-history exercises with unresolved errors per
benchmark and compare a fully teacher-generated action with teacher
continuations conditioned on the student’s reasoning, or on its
reasoning plus half of its operation. We measure continuation
*Executability* and *Appropriateness*. Both decline as more
student-generated prefix is retained
(Table [8](#A1.T8.fig1 "Table 8 ‣ A.2.2 Stage 1: Analysis ‣ A.2 Experiment results ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?"));
with half the operation retained, appropriateness drops from 80.2% to
56.2% for Qwen3-8B and from 83.8% to 60.2% for Qwen3-14B. Thus, student
prefixes can constrain the teacher into less useful continuations even
at the same history.

##### History sources change where teacher and student disagree ($`TS`$ vs. $`SS`$).

At rounds 1, 3, 5, and 8, we sample 100 exercises per configuration
containing an explicit error without subsequent self-correction (see
details in
Appendix [A.1.4](#A1.SS1.SSS4 "A.1.4 Trajectory Annotation Protocols ‣ A.1 Additional details on experiment setup ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?")).
We compute mean per-token KL before, within, and after the first
annotated error span, then normalize the three regional means by their
sum. Under $`TS`$, disagreement concentrates on the error span, whereas
$`SS`$ assigns relatively more disagreement before the error
(Figure [8](#A1.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ A.2.2 Stage 1: Analysis ‣ A.2 Experiment results ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?")).
Teacher histories therefore produce more error-localized disagreement,
while student histories distribute disagreement more broadly across the
action.

#### 4.2.2 Behavior of trained students

##### Configurations learn different behavioral strengths.

For 80 test tasks per benchmark, we annotate one trajectory per
configuration using five nonexclusive error categories: repeated
failure, premature completion, rule inconsistency, operational mistakes
despite correct plans, and high-level planning mistakes. $`SS`$ exhibits
fewer repeated failures and planning mistakes, whereas $`TT`$ follows
explicit rules more reliably
(Table [7](#A1.T7 "Table 7 ‣ A.2.2 Stage 1: Analysis ‣ A.2 Experiment results ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?")).

##### $`ST`$ is strongest at recovering from student errors.

For Qwen3-14B, we resume all four trained policies from the same 100
erroneous initial-model histories per benchmark on ToolQA, ALFWorld, and
WebShop. $`ST`$ achieves the highest rates of both error correction and
eventual task success
(Figure [7](#A1.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ A.2.2 Stage 1: Analysis ‣ A.2 Experiment results ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?")).
Although $`TT`$ and $`TS`$ outperform $`SS`$ from task starts, their
eventual success from erroneous histories is similar to $`SS`$. Their
standard-evaluation advantage therefore does not translate into stronger
recovery. $`ST`$ uniquely combines exposure to student mistakes with
teacher-generated corrective actions.

##### Configurations also differ in learning dynamics.

For Qwen3-14B on ToolQA, ALFWorld, and WebShop, $`TT`$ leads during
rounds 1–3, $`ST`$ overtakes it by round 5 and finishes highest, while
$`SS`$ improves more gradually and continues gaining later in training
(Figure [6](#A1.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ A.2.2 Stage 1: Analysis ‣ A.2 Experiment results ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?")).
These complementary behaviors motivate mixture design in Stage 2 and
scheduling in Stage 3.

## 5 Stage 2: Pairing and training-mixture study

Stage 1 favors $`ST`$ as a standalone configuration, but weaker
configurations may provide complementary supervision when mixed. We
therefore study how the four configurations should be paired and
allocated under a fixed training budget. All mixtures match the total
number of exercises and training rounds and reuse the initial Stage 1
exercise pools. We order mixture weights as $`(TT,ST,TS,SS)`$.

### 5.1 Pairing Matters at Fixed On-Policiness

We compare three mixtures with identical marginal on-policiness:
$`w_{\mathrm{Diagonal}}=(0.5,0,0,0.5)`$,
$`w_{\mathrm{Crossed}}=(0,0.5,0.5,0)`$, and
$`w_{\mathrm{Independent}}=(0.25,0.25,0.25,0.25)`$. Each assigns 50% of
examples to student histories and 50% to student action prefixes,
differing only in how the two sources are paired.

Figure [2](#S5.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 5.1 Pairing Matters at Fixed On-Policiness ‣ 5 Stage 2: Pairing and training-mixture study ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?")
shows Qwen3-14B results; other backbones are in
Appendix [A.2.4](#A1.SS2.SSS4 "A.2.4 Stage 2 Main results (cont.) ‣ A.2 Experiment results ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?").
The independent mixture performs best across all shown metrics and
benchmarks and improves success rate over standalone $`ST`$ by 0.5–3.3
points. Thus, marginal on-policiness alone is insufficient: the joint
pairing of history and prefix sources also matters.

Figure 2: Pairing at fixed marginal on-policiness with Qwen3-14B. Dashed
lines indicate standalone $`ST`$ performance from Stage 1.

### 5.2 From Complementarity to Mixture Composition

##### Retain both $`TT`$ and $`SS`$.

Holding $`ST`$ and $`TS`$ at 0.25 each, we compare *TT-more*,
$`(0.5,0.25,0.25,0)`$, and *SS-more*, $`(0,0.25,0.25,0.5)`$, against the
independent mixture. Across all settings, the independent mixture
outperforms both, while TT-more outperforms SS-more
(Figures [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Retain both 𝑇⁢𝑇 and 𝑆⁢𝑆. ‣ 5.2 From Complementarity to Mixture Composition ‣ 5 Stage 2: Pairing and training-mixture study ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?"),
[11](#A1.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ A.2.5 Stage 2: TT and SS contributions decomposition ‣ A.2 Experiment results ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?"),
and
[12](#A1.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ A.2.5 Stage 2: TT and SS contributions decomposition ‣ A.2 Experiment results ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?")).
Thus, retaining both diagonal configurations is more effective than
assigning their combined budget entirely to either one. In particular,
adding some $`SS`$ improves over TT-more despite $`SS`$’s weak
standalone performance. The TT-more–SS-more gap is smaller for Qwen3-14B
than for Qwen3-8B, consistent with the smaller model’s greater
sensitivity to fully on-policy training.

Figure 3: Retaining both diagonal configurations improves success rate
with Qwen3-14B. Holding $`ST`$ and $`TS`$ at 0.25 each, the remaining
allocation is assigned to $`TT`$ only (TT-more), $`SS`$ only (SS-more),
or equally to both (Independent)

##### Emphasize hybrid configurations without removing the diagonals.

We increase the combined weight of $`ST`$ and $`TS`$ from 0.5 to 0.75,
yielding the *hybrid-heavy* mixture $`(0.125,0.375,0.375,0.125)`$. It
improves success rate over the independent mixture in every setting
(Table [9](#A1.T9.fig1 "Table 9 ‣ A.2.7 Stage 2: Hybrid configuration ‣ A.2 Experiment results ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?")).
However, removing $`TT`$ and $`SS`$ entirely, as in the crossed mixture,
performs worse than the independent mixture. These results favor
emphasizing hybrid configurations while retaining complementary $`TT`$
and $`SS`$ examples.

##### Favor student histories over student action prefixes.

Finally, we ask how to divide the hybrid allocation. Keeping $`TT`$ and
$`SS`$ at 0.125 each, we compare *ST-more*, $`(0.125,0.5,0.25,0.125)`$,
against *TS-more*, $`(0.125,0.25,0.5,0.125)`$. These mixtures exchange
the student-history and student-prefix proportions, while preserving the
combined hybrid allocation. ST-more yields higher success rate in every
setting
(Figure [13](#A1.F13 "Figure 13 ‣ A.2.6 Stage 2: ST vs TS ‣ A.2 Experiment results ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?")),
extending the directional preference observed from Stage 1 to this mixed
training.

The resulting principle of these comparisons is to emphasize student
histories paired with teacher actions without excluding configurations
that are weaker in isolation.

## 6 Stage 3: Scheduling the Training Mixture

Stage 2 shows that mixture composition matters, but should the same
allocation be maintained throughout learning? The dynamics analysis in
Stage 1 suggest otherwise: $`TT`$ supports rapid initial progress,
whereas $`SS`$ improves more slowly and continues gaining later. We
therefore investigate whether emphasizing these configurations at
different stages improves mixed training.

We use the independent mixture, $`(0.25,0.25,0.25,0.25)`$, as a balanced
reference and compare its static allocation with three schedules over 8
training rounds. *TT-first* places approximately 80% of the total $`TT`$
allocation in rounds 1–4 and the remaining 20% in rounds 5–8. *SS-later*
reverses this split for $`SS`$, allocating 20% early and 80% late.
*TT-first + SS-later* combines both schedules. Each targeted
configuration retains its total allocation across training. We measure
validation success rate after every round on ToolQA, ALFWorld, and
WebShop
(Figure [4](#S6.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 6 Stage 3: Scheduling the Training Mixture ‣ Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?")).

$`TT`$-first accelerates initial learning on all three benchmarks: by
round 4, its success rate exceeds the static baseline by 8.7–13.2
percentage points. Its final advantage is smaller, at 0.7–2.0 points. In
contrast, $`SS`$-later initially trails the static baseline on ToolQA
and WebShop and closely tracks it on ALFWorld, but overtakes it during
the second half of training and finishes 2.0–2.9 points higher. The two
schedules therefore offer distinct benefits: front-loading $`TT`$
improves early progress, while delaying $`SS`$ yields a larger
improvement in final performance.

The combined schedule outperforms the static baseline at all evaluated
training rounds and achieves the highest final validation success rate
among the tested schedules on all three benchmarks. Although
$`TT`$-first alone often leads early, the combined schedule ultimately
surpasses it. These results suggest complementary temporal roles:
teacher-generated contexts support rapid initial learning, while greater
exposure to fully on-policy contexts is more beneficial later. They
favor front-loading $`TT`$ and delaying $`SS`$ within a mixture, rather
than maintaining a uniform allocation throughout training.

Figure 4: Validation success rate across eight training rounds under
static and scheduled allocations of the independent mixture. initial
denotes the initial student.

##### Conclusions across the three stages.

Across the three stages, effective on-policiness depends on *where*,
*how much*, and *when* student-generated context is used. Student
histories paired with teacher actions provide the strongest standalone
performance and recovery, while mixed training benefits from retaining
configurations that are weaker in isolation. Scheduling $`TT`$ earlier
and $`SS`$ later further improves over a static mixture. Thus, effective
agent distillation depends not on maximizing on-policy data, but on how
it is sourced, combined, and scheduled.

## 7 Related Work

##### Distillation and privileged information for agents.

Knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from a teacher model to a
student model ([Hinton et al., 2015](#bib.bib1)). Demonstration-based
approaches improve LLM agents through supervised training on interaction
trajectories ([Zeng et al., 2024](#bib.bib10)), while context
distillation transfers behaviors elicited by additional instructions or
reasoning context into a model that no longer requires such context at
inference time ([Snell et al., 2022](#bib.bib23); [Gao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib24)). For interactive agents, [Alakuijala et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib4) internalize task guidance and corrective feedback
through iterative distillation, whereas [Wang et al. (2026)](#bib.bib14)
use trajectory-derived skills as privileged teacher context for
on-policy self-distillation. Our work addresses the complementary
question of how teacher- and student-generated contexts should be
constructed, combined, and scheduled when distilling privileged
guidance.

##### On-policy distillation and imitation learning.

On-policy distillation (OPD) ([Agarwal et al., 2024](#bib.bib9))
mitigates training–deployment mismatch by obtaining teacher supervision
on student-generated sequences, and has become increasingly common in
LLM post-training ([Lu and Lab, 2025](#bib.bib7); [Zhao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib13)). For multi-turn agents, however, student-generated
interactions may reach states for which the teacher cannot provide
reliable supervision. Concurrent work, ReOPD ([Liao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib25)), addresses this issue by generating student actions
from replayed teacher histories, enabling teacher supervision without
requiring new environment interactions during student training. Related
challenges arise in imitation learning ([Ross et al.,
2011](#bib.bib15)), where expert supervision is collected on
learner-visited states to mitigate sequential distribution shift. Our
framework distinguishes history-level and action-prefix-level
on-policiness as separate but coupled design choices, thereby unifying
teacher-generated, student-generated, and hybrid contexts under a common
objective. This formulation enables controlled analysis of their
individual effects, their interactions in mixed training regimes, and
their allocation over the course of training.

## 8 Conclusion

We introduced hierarchical agent distillation framework that formalizes
on-policiness at the history and action-prefix levels. Across three
backbones and four interactive environments, student-induced histories
paired with teacher-generated actions generally provide the strongest
standalone performance. Mixture comparisons show that pairing matters
even when marginal on-policiness is fixed, and that configurations
weaker in isolation can improve mixed training. Scheduling experiments
further show that emphasizing fully teacher-generated contexts early and
fully on-policy contexts later improves validation performance over a
static uniform mixture. Together, these findings move agent distillation
beyond a binary on-policy/off-policy choice: effective training depends
on where the student is followed, how teacher and student contexts are
paired, and when each configuration is emphasized.

##### Limitation.

Our experiments focus on privileged-information-based self-distillation
with frozen teachers initialized from the same checkpoints as the
students. Generalization to substantially larger models remains to be
established. Also, the mixture study identifies composition principles
through targeted comparisons rather than a universally optimal
allocation.

### AI use statement

We used large language models to assist with manuscript writing and
editing, as well as in parts of the experimental pipeline, including
annotating agent trajectories and constructing task guidance.
AI-assisted outputs used in the experiments were generated following the
procedures described in the paper and appendix and were reviewed or
validated as appropriate. The authors remain responsible for the study
design, experimental analysis, interpretation of results, and final
manuscript.

#### A.1.2 Benchmarks

We evaluate on four interactive agent benchmarks spanning tool-augmented
question answering, office automation, embodied household tasks, and web
interaction.

- •
  ToolQA. ToolQA ([Zhuang et al., 2023](#bib.bib19)) evaluates an
  agent’s ability to answer questions by retrieving and reasoning over
  information from external data sources with heterogeneous formats,
  including text documents, graphs, and tabular databases. Following the
  processed version of [Alakuijala et al. (2026)](#bib.bib4), we
  consider six task groups: DBLP, Agenda, Yelp, Airbnb, Flight, and
  Coffee. The agent has access to nine tools for querying and processing
  the corresponding data sources, while individual task groups typically
  require only a subset of these tools.
- •
  OfficeBench. OfficeBench ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib20)) evaluates
  an agent’s ability to complete multi-step office workflows involving
  six applications: Email, Calendar, Word, Excel, OCR, and PDF Reader.
  The agent has access to 20 tools for interacting with these
  applications. Tasks can involve one to three applications, requiring
  the agent to plan across multiple steps, select appropriate tools, and
  transfer information between applications.
- •
  ALFWorld. ALFWorld ([Shridhar et al., 2021](#bib.bib21)) is a
  text-based embodied environment in which an agent follows
  natural-language instructions to perform household tasks through
  sequential interaction with objects and receptacles. We consider its
  six commonly used task categories: Pick & Place, Pick Two & Place,
  Clean & Place, Heat & Place, Cool & Place, and Examine in Light.
  Completing a task requires the agent to explore the environment,
  locate relevant objects, and execute an appropriate sequence of
  navigation and manipulation actions, such as picking up, placing,
  cleaning, heating, or cooling objects.
- •
  WebShop. WebShop ([Yao et al., 2022a](#bib.bib22)) is a simulated
  e-commerce environment that evaluates agents on interactive web
  navigation and product search. Given a natural-language shopping
  instruction specifying desired product properties and constraints, the
  agent must search for candidate products, navigate between search and
  product pages, inspect product information and available options, and
  purchase an item that best satisfies the instruction. The environment
  exposes two main types of actions, search\[query\] and
  click\[option\], requiring the agent to perform query formulation,
  information gathering, comparison, and multi-step decision making.

#### A.1.4 Trajectory Annotation Protocols

We use a two-stage annotation protocol. The first stage identifies
exercises that satisfy the prerequisite for a given analysis, such as
containing an issue that remains unresolved in the history. The second
stage performs issue- or action-level annotation on the retained
exercises. We primarily use Qwen3-235B-A22B as the annotator and use
GPT-5.4 to adjudicate cases for which the primary annotator returns
Uncertain.

##### Identifying exercises with unresolved issues.

For each sampled exercise, we provide the complete interaction history
to Qwen3-235B-A22B and ask it to identify all issues encountered during
the trajectory and summarize how the agent responds to each issue. An
issue may correspond, for example, to an incorrect intermediate
decision, a failed operation, or a constraint revealed by environment
feedback. Based on this analysis, the annotator determines whether at
least one identified issue remains unresolved at the point of interest.
It outputs one of three labels: Yes, No, or Uncertain, together with the
identified issues and a brief summary of the attempted or completed
resolution for each issue. Exercises labeled Uncertain are reassessed by
GPT-5.4, which receives the original exercise together with the complete
annotation produced by Qwen3-235B-A22B.

##### Annotating issue-specific agent behavior.

After selecting exercises satisfying the prerequisite of the
corresponding analysis, we perform more targeted annotations of the
agent’s behavior. Depending on the diagnostic, we use the following
procedures:

- •
  Issue recognition and corrective behavior. We ask Qwen3-235B-A22B to
  determine whether the reasoning segment of the current action
  explicitly recognizes an issue present in the preceding history. If an
  issue is recognized, the annotator further determines whether the
  action (i) resolves the issue or (ii) takes an appropriate corrective
  step toward resolving it. We additionally provide the task-specific
  privileged information used in our distillation framework as reference
  information to help the annotator interpret the task requirements and
  the intended solution procedure. Cases labeled Uncertain are
  reassessed by GPT-5.4.
- •
  Quality of the proposed correction. For annotations requiring a
  judgment about the quality of an action—for example, whether a
  proposed correction is executable and appropriate, or whether the
  action constitutes a valid self-correction—we use a solution-first
  annotation procedure. Before evaluating the agent’s action, the
  annotator is first asked to independently derive an appropriate next
  step given the task history and available task information. It then
  evaluates the agent’s proposed action relative to this independently
  derived solution. We found this decomposition to produce more reliable
  judgments than directly asking the annotator to assess action quality.
````
